content: Cardiac Rehabilitation (Patient Information) Overview Participating in a cardiac rehabilitation program can provide numerous benefits for your heart health and overall well-being. These include: Gaining a comprehensive understanding of the risk factors associated with heart disease and learning effective strategies to reduce them. Developing techniques to better manage stress, including anger management, which can positively impact your cardiovascular health. Learning about the mechanisms of action, therapeutic effects, potential side effects, and possible drug interactions of your prescribed medications. Enhancing the strength and efficiency of your heart and cardiovascular system through tailored physical activity. Experiencing an improved sense of well-being and self-confidence as you progress through the program. Increasing your ability to engage in daily physical activities with greater ease and endurance. What to Eat at the Restaurant? When dining out, it is important to make heart-healthy choices. Consider the following recommendations: Inquire about low-fat or fat-free options on the menu. Request substitutions, such as steamed vegetables in place of French fries. Follow the principles of your healthy eating plan when selecting a main course. Opt for lean proteins like fish, skinless chicken, or lean cuts of meat. Choose entrées that are prepared using healthier cooking methods, such as broiling, baking, grilling, steaming, or poaching, rather than frying. Select vegetable-based side dishes and ask for any sauces or butter to be omitted. Request low-calorie salad dressings or use a lemon wedge to add flavor to your salad instead of traditional dressings. Choose baked, boiled, or roasted potatoes instead of fried options, and ask for them to be served without butter or sour cream. For dessert, opt for fresh fruit or fruit sorbet instead of calorie-dense options like cake, pie, or ice cream. If the menu seems to lack suitable options, ask the chef if they can prepare a fruit or vegetable platter for you. Most chefs are willing to accommodate such requests. What to Avoid at the Restaurant? To maintain a heart-healthy diet while eating out, avoid the following: Move the butter away from your table or request that it be replaced with soft margarine. Ask for dressings and sauces to be served on the side so you can control the amount you consume. Avoid fried appetizers and creamy soups. Instead, start your meal with a broth-based soup, such as minestrone or gazpacho. At salad bars, steer clear of high-fat toppings like cheese, creamy dressings, chopped eggs, croutons, olives, and bacon bits. Request that your food be prepared without butter or cream-based sauces. You may find that broiled meat, fish, or chicken prepared dry can be just as flavorful. Remove the skin from poultry and trim visible fat from meat before eating. Additional Resources For further guidance on lifestyle modifications and risk reduction strategies, refer to the recommendations provided by the American Heart Association.
